evidence.claim: A river runs between the roadways of an early automobile parkway
evidence.quote: the roadways diverge and the river runs between them.

evidence.claim: The Bronx River Parkway follows its namesake river through Westchester, with wooded stretches and roadways that separate with the river between them.
evidence.quote: The roadways remain apart through a wooded section

evidence.claim: Its 13.2-mile Westchester section, from the Bronx county line to Kensico Dam Plaza, is a New York State Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: The section of the Bronx River Parkway within Westchester County is a designated New York State Scenic Byway, from the Bronx – Westchester County line to the Kensico Dam Plaza.

evidence.claim: NYSDOT identifies scenic, historical and recreational qualities, including the road’s pioneering use of a median and bridges for crossing streets.
evidence.quote: Themes: Scenic, Historical, Scenic, Recreational

evidence.claim: North of White Plains, junctions are controlled by traffic lights.
evidence.quote: North of White Plains, all interchanges are at-grade intersections with traffic lights.

evidence.claim: Construction began in Westchester in 1907, making this the country’s earliest limited-access automobile route to begin construction.
evidence.quote: Construction began in Westchester County in 1907. This makes it the earliest limited access automobile route to start construction in the United States.

evidence.claim: The Long Island Motor Parkway started a year later but opened a section in 1908, before the Bronx River road.
evidence.quote: although construction on the Long Island Motor Parkway began a year later, a section of the Long Island road opened for traffic before the end of 1908, opening before the Bronx River Parkway

evidence.claim: After delays, the remaining Westchester construction began in 1917; sections opened in 1922 and 1925.
evidence.quote: Construction on the remainder of the portion in Westchester began in 1917, after almost a decade of delays. The first of this opened in 1922, with the last opened in 1925.

evidence.claim: Later rebuilding widened the stretch between Bronxville and the Bronx and replaced intersections with overpasses or separated interchanges.
evidence.quote: In 1953, reconstruction and widening to six lanes began the 2.6-mile (4.2 km) segment between Bronxville and the Bronx.

evidence.claim: Start southbound at Kensico Circle, within sight of the dam, and follow the river-and-rail corridor toward White Plains.
evidence.quote: Kensico Dam is visible in the distance as the parkway reaches its northern terminus at Kensico Circle

evidence.claim: Continue through Scarsdale to the wooded separation of the roadways in Yonkers.
evidence.quote: The roadways remain apart through a wooded section as they curve westward for the next three-quarter mile, returning to the highway's northeastern heading as it leaves Yonkers and briefly enters Greenburgh south of the southbound Ardsley Road exit east of downtown Scarsdale.

evidence.claim: Below the Sprain Brook junction at Bronxville, the road takes on its controlled-access commuter character.
evidence.quote: In Westchester County, the road continues to have the same character until the Sprain Brook Parkway splits off at Bronxville

evidence.claim: The scenic designation ends at the Bronx line, although the parkway continues south.
evidence.quote: from the Bronx – Westchester County line to the Kensico Dam Plaza.

evidence.claim: Its 13.2-mile Westchester section
evidence.quote: Length: 13.2 miles

evidence.claim: including the road’s pioneering use of a median and bridges for crossing streets.
evidence.quote: The Bronx River Parkway was the first highway to utilize a median strip to separate opposing lanes, the first highway constructed through a park, the Bronx River Reservation, and the first highway where intersecting streets crossed over bridges.

evidence.claim: replaced intersections with overpasses or separated interchanges.
evidence.quote: Intersections in the area were also replaced by overpasses or grade separated interchanges.

evidence.claim: follow the river-and-rail corridor toward White Plains.
evidence.quote: Halfway through the borough it begins to closely parallel the Harlem Line of Metro-North Railroad, a pairing which continues to the road's northern terminus.

evidence.claim: although the parkway continues south.
evidence.quote: The southern terminus of the parkway is at Story Avenue near the Bruckner Expressway in the Bronx neighborhood of Soundview.

evidence.claim: Kensico Dam rises 307 feet above its foundation at the parkway’s northern end.
evidence.quote: The dam is 1,843 feet (562 m) long, stands 307 feet (94 m) above its foundation

evidence.claim: The earlier dam, built in 1885, could not meet New York’s growing demand for water.
evidence.quote: The dam formed a small lake with water from the Bronx and Byram Rivers, but it was not enough for New York's increasing population.

evidence.claim: Demolition began in 1911; construction of the replacement followed in 1913 and finished in 1917, three years ahead of schedule.
evidence.quote: Before constructing the new Kensico Dam, the old one had to be removed; demolition began in 1911. The construction of the new dam began in 1913 and was concluded in 1917—three years ahead of schedule

evidence.claim: The reservoir required the flooding of Kensico village, whose families moved to surrounding communities after their land was condemned and appraised.
evidence.quote: Many of the families had to move to the surrounding communities of Armonk, Harrison, Valhalla, and White Plains. The village of Kensico was then flooded to make way for the reservoir.

evidence.claim: History placards now stand throughout the plaza at the foot of the dam.
evidence.quote: Placards posted throughout the plaza encompass its history.

evidence.claim: The earlier dam, built in 1885
evidence.quote: In 1885, the old Kensico Dam was built south of the village of Kensico

evidence.claim: after their land was condemned and appraised.
evidence.quote: each individual lot of land was condemned and appraised

evidence.claim: at the parkway’s northern end.
evidence.quote: Kensico Dam is visible in the distance as the parkway reaches its northern terminus at Kensico Circle

evidence.claim: Near the Cross Westchester Expressway, the parkway’s two roadways spread almost 400 feet apart before coming together again at Old Tarrytown Road.
evidence.quote: The two roadways once again diverge, becoming almost 400 feet (120 m) apart in the half-mile (1 km) before they converge again as they reach the Old Tarrytown Road intersection just north of the expressway.

evidence.claim: Farther south, the road passes the developed western edge of downtown White Plains.
evidence.quote: just west of the White Plains station on the west side of heavily developed downtown White Plains.

evidence.claim: White Plains became the county seat in 1758.
evidence.quote: In 1758, White Plains became the seat of Westchester County

evidence.claim: Its postwar shopping district drew customers from beyond the city as nearby parkways and expressways were built.
evidence.quote: Construction of nearby parkways and expressways in the 1940s through the 1970s brought shoppers from elsewhere.

evidence.claim: The Bronx River Parkway crosses both the river and the railroad tracks within the city.
evidence.quote: After the northbound Walworth crossing exit, it turns northwest across the river and the tracks

evidence.claim: In the wooded stretch north of Leewood Drive, the Bronx River flows between the parkway’s separated roadways.
evidence.quote: One-tenth of a mile (160 m) to the north, the roadways diverge and the river runs between them.

evidence.claim: The roadways curve through woods before drawing back toward the railway corridor at Crestwood.
evidence.quote: The roadways remain apart through a wooded section as they curve westward

evidence.claim: Building the parkway changed the neighborhood as well as the river corridor.
evidence.quote: The construction of the Bronx River Parkway had a profound effect on the geography of the Crestwood/Tuckahoe area.

evidence.claim: Right-of-way purchases took Crestwood lots and divided cross streets.
evidence.quote: As part of the right-of-way purchases, lots belonging to Crestwood were bought and cross roads were divided into two.

evidence.claim: The Bronx River also separates Crestwood, in Yonkers, from the village of Tuckahoe.
evidence.quote: Located in northeastern Yonkers, Crestwood is separated by the Bronx River from the village of Tuckahoe.

evidence.claim: The Harlem Line follows the river, with its Crestwood station named for the neighborhood across the water.
evidence.quote: the northern station Crestwood for the Crestwood neighborhood to the west, in Yonkers.

evidence.claim: before drawing back toward the railway corridor at Crestwood.
evidence.quote: Exit 8, Thompson Street, serves the nearby Crestwood station as the Harlem Line's tracks begin to parallel the road again.

evidence.claim: Engineer Frank E. Winsor directed construction, with crews made up largely of Italian immigrants.
evidence.quote: Frank E. Winsor was the engineer in charge of construction at Kensico.

evidence.claim: with crews made up largely of Italian immigrants.
evidence.quote: Crews were largely made up of Italian immigrants

evidence.claim: At the County Center, Central Avenue meets the parkway at a junction controlled by traffic lights.
evidence.quote: at-grade intersections with traffic lights, also signed and numbered as exits, with Central Avenue (NY 100), at the Westchester County Center.

evidence.quote: the roadways diverge and the river runs between them.

evidence.claim: The nearby Crestwood station appeared on the cover of The Saturday Evening Post in 1946, in Norman Rockwell’s painting Commuters.
evidence.quote: This train station was depicted on the cover of The Saturday Evening Post issue for November 16, 1946, in the painting Commuters, by Norman Rockwell.
